text: MEASURE P CITY ATTORNEY'S IMPARTIAL ANALYSIS
This measure was placed on the ballot following receipt of a petition signed by the requisite number of registered voters of the City of Menlo Park ("City").

If adopted, the measure would add a new Title 17 to the Menlo Park Municipal Code entitled "Downtown Parking Plazas Ordinance" ("Measure"). The Measure identifies eight City-owned parking plazas in downtown Menlo Park ("Parking Plazas").

The Measure provides that the City may not take certain actions that would diminish the availability of, access to, or convenience of parking on the Parking Plazas, without voter approval. Specifically, if the City wishes to take any of the following actions ("Action(s)"), the City must take all legally required steps to approve the Action and then place such Action on the next regularly scheduled election ballot, and such Action will only become effective if approved by a majority of the voters:

Selling, trading, leasing, donating, disposing of, or otherwise conveying a Parking Plaza or portion thereof; Designating a Parking Plaza as "surplus land" or "exempt surplus land" under the Surplus Land Act (Government Code section 54220 et seq.); Modifying, altering, or constructing improvements on a Parking Plaza that permanently diminish parking; or Changing the use of a Parking Plaza to diminish parking.

The Measure provides that voter approval is not required for: (1) maintenance, repairs, renovations, or capital improvements intended to preserve, improve, or expand parking availability, access, or convenience, even if those activities temporarily affect parking; or (2) temporary community activities, such as farmers' markets, lasting no more than three consecutive days.

Under existing law, the City Council determines the uses of City-owned property, including the Parking Plazas. The Measure provides instead that the City is prohibited from taking any of the Actions without voter approval.

The Measure provides that it is retroactive, and that if the City takes an Action between May 15, 2025 and the Ordinance's effective date, such Action shall be null and void, unless the Action is reenacted in compliance with the Ordinance and approved by the voters.

The Measure provides that it operates notwithstanding any other provision of the City's Municipal Code, General Plan, or the El Camino Real/Downtown Specific Plan. The City's Housing Element includes Program H4.G, which plans for the development of at least 345 affordable housing units on some combination of the Parking Plazas. The Measure provides that voter approval is required before the City could implement Program H4.G to develop affordable housing if it would diminish access to or convenience of public parking.
The Measure may be amended or repealed only by a vote of the people. A "yes" vote approves the Measure. A "no" vote rejects it.

text: Vote YES! on Measure _ to give voters a say before the City Council can permanently convert downtown parking plazas into high-rise developments.
A FLAWED PLAN Over 3,000 Menlo Park residents signed the Measure X petition because they don't believe Council's plan is an effective way to provide the low-income housing we need.

Council presumed that developers, who'd get the plazas for $1 [year, could pay to replace 556 spaces. But the developer proposals tell a different story, and Menlo Park could be on the hook for tens of millions to build public garages. Furthermore, the City's done insufficient analysis on economic impact, traffic, parking, overcrowded classrooms, or fire safety.
Already, 135 downtown businesses publicly oppose the Council's plan, as they'd be unlikely to survive years of high-rise construction followed by a permanent loss of convenient parking.

A SMARTER WAY FORWARD Most residents aren't aware, but Menlo Park is proving it can deliver housing without this plan. Menlo Park's own July 2026 housing update reported that housing capacity exceeds state requirements by 30%. Since 2010, Menlo Park has added more than 1 ,400 homes, nearly 30% more growth than the county average.

And 1 , 750 more homes are on the way, near downtown, at the former SRI and USGS sites. The problem is that not enough of them are affordable to local workers. We can remedy that by incentivizing the developers to shift units to the very-low- income category. The City's cost to do that would be far less than giving away public land, building expensive garages, and undermining local businesses.
Menlo Park has many ways to meet its housing goals. The greatest risk is Council pushing forward, without community consent, with a flawed, unfunded plan that could fail us all.
Vote YES! on Measure It ensures our voices are heard.

text: Vote No on Measure X to protect Affordable Homes and support a vibrant downtown small business district in Menlo Park!

Menlo Park is one of the most expensive communities in the country. Teachers, caregivers, firefighters, and emergency responders cannot afford to live here. The next generation deserves the chance to stay near family and friends. Yet, every day, it gets harder to afford a home.

Downtown Menlo Park has too many empty storefronts. Redwood City, San Carlos, and Burlingame have seen a boom in downtown businesses after adding housing and improving parking. New homes bring activity, vitality, and business to downtown. Measure X would prevent Menlo Park from doing this.

If approved, Measure X would block Menlo Park's ability to replace aging surface parking lots with modern garages and add affordable homes above. Measure X inhibits bicycle and pedestrian safety improvements. All told, Measure X would make it harder for families, seniors, and people with disabilities to live and visit downtown.

Measure X is bad policy with no expiration date. Independent analysis finds it likely violates state laws, risking millions in legal fees and years of delay. Taxpayers would foot the bill to defend it, including endless appeals (no matter the merits). It could also put Menlo Park out of compliance with state housing law, costing local control of development (and allowing builder's remedy projects) city-wide.
If approved, Measure X would:

Block affordable homes downtown. Hinder Menlo Park's efforts to revitalize downtown like neighboring cities have. Block much-needed downtown parking improvements. Forever inhibit the city's ability to plan for downtown's future. Delay even simple downtown projects like installing EV Chargers, by up to two years. Complicate compliance with state law. Cost Menlo Park taxpayers millions in legal fees.
Join trusted community leaders and organizations and Vote No on Measure X to support a vibrant downtown and create affordable homes within reach for Menlo Park!

text: Rebuttal to the Argument in Favor of Measure P 245/250 Words
Don't let the group proposing this measure fool you. Voting for Measure P will NOT save downtown, will NOT improve parking, and will NOT create affordable homes.

This small group prioritizes inefficient parking lots over the community's needs. They ignore vacant storefronts. They ignore the young families, seniors, teachers, nurses, firefighters, city staff, retail employees, and others who are priced out of Menlo Park.

Measure P will block affordable homes and convenient, modern parking downtown. Measure P risks losing local control city-wide because, despite what the proponents say, the city's annual report shows that the downtown sites are essential to the city's plan for affordable homes. 13 Measure P ignores reality and the need to address housing costs in Menlo Park. Unnecessary barriers will only worsen our affordability crisis. Our community cannot afford Measure P.

Measure P includes a poison pill: if anyone sues over this measure, only the three people who put it on the ballot — not voters, not City Council — get to make the final decision about defending it. But Menlo Park taxpayers pay the legal fees.

Measure P supporters say building housing downtown will hurt business. This is FALSE. As we have seen in neighboring communities, improving parking and adding housing means more small businesses and more customers.
Measure P would interfere with the City's decision-making process related to City-owned downtown parking lot properties, including improvements.
Measure P is bad policy that makes our community more expensive and less accessible.
Join us, Congressman Sam Liccardo, and Habitat for Humanity in voting NO on Measure P to 3 save Downtown Menlo Park!
City Manager's Office

text: Don't be fooled by misleading claims. Vote YES! on Measure P to meet our housing goals without sacrificing our downtown. As long-time Menlo Park residents and civic leaders, we're committed to affordable housing. Together, we can do it right. q Measure P enables a more reliable path to affordable homes. Council's plan is already failing. We have better options. More than 1 , 750 additional homes 16 are being planned on major sites near downtown. And talks are underway to convert the 25-acre office park off Marsh Rd. to housing. Let's work with those developers to make more units affordable. It would be less costly, and less damaging, than building from 5 scratch on tiny, congested plazas. Measure P keeps our downtown accessible. (3 The parking plazas support our community and the viability of our downtown. Measure P IL-I gives you a vote before they're converted into urban-style, 6-8 story high-rises, with insufficient parking for the new residents, and no explanation of who'd pay to replace the current public parking - taxpayers would be on the hook for N$50M. 6 Measure P is simple and reasonable. Measure P doesn't block development on the plazas — it merely requires voter approval. It expressly allows improvements to the "availability, access, or convenience" of parking - 16 without a vote.
